The opening with the interrogative about the arrival of the report of al-Ghashiyah is used to create eagerness (tashwiq) to know this report, because of the admonition that follows from it.

It was called "the overwhelming" by way of metaphor (isti'arah, a figure in which a term is transferred to a new meaning on the basis of resemblance), because when it occurs people will find no escape from its terrors, so it is as if it were a covering that overwhelms their minds. The indefinite form of "wujuh" as subject is intended to denote a category.

"Khashi'a, 'amila, nasiba" are three predicates of "wujuh," and the meaning is: people who are humbled, etc.

"Wujuh" is a kinaya (metonymy) for their owners, since the face is used to denote the self, as in His words: ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord, Full of Majesty and Honor.﴾ [al-Rahman: 27]. The indicator of this here is His words after it, ﴿they will have no food except from a bitter thorny plant,﴾ since the pronoun referring to "wujuh" is treated as a plural of rational beings.

"Wujuh" is chosen for the kinaya of their owners here and in similar contexts, because the condition of the faces indicates the condition of their owners. The face is the sign of what its owner experiences of bliss or misery, as one says: "He went out with a face other than the one he went in with."

This was discussed earlier in His words: ﴿Faces that Day will be bright﴾ [Abasa: 38], in Surah Abasa.

It is permissible to take the attribution of humility, labor, and exhaustion to "wujuh" as majaz 'aqli (rational or attributive metaphor), meaning: the owners of faces.

Since "idh" is one of the words that must be followed by a clause, the clause it is attached to is omitted, and tanwin replaces it. What indicates it is the sense of the epithet in the name "al-Ghashiya," which retains the original sense of an adjective, for it means "that which overwhelms people." So the omitted clause is estimated as: "on the Day when the Overwhelming Event overwhelms."

Or the context of the speech indicates the clause, so it is estimated as: "on the Day when it occurs or takes place."

The clause ﴿they will have no food...﴾ and so on is a sixth predicate of "wujuh."

The pronoun in "lahum" refers to "wujuh" in view of its interpretation as "the owners of faces," and therefore the masculine plural pronoun is used. The masculine form is taghlib (predominance), giving precedence to males over females.

"Al-dari'" is the dried part of the shibriq, with a kasra on the shin, a sukun on the ba', and a kasra on the ra'. It is a thorny plant when fresh, and when it dries it is called "dari'," and then it becomes poisonous. It is pasture for camels and wild donkeys when it is fresh. It may also be derived from n'ima, with the vowel of the 'ayn being i, yan'am, like hadhira, when one possesses blessing, that is: of good living and affluence.

Li-sa'yiha (for their striving) is connected to the word radiyah (pleased), and radiyah is a second predicate of wujuh.

What is meant by sa'y (striving) is the work that a person strives at in order to benefit from it. He expressed it here as the counterpart to his saying regarding its opposite, 'amilah (laboring).

Al-Ridha (contentment) is the opposite of anger, that is: they praise what they strove for in this world of the work which is the carrying out of what Allah commanded through the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ).

The prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿in a lofty Garden﴾ is a third predicate of wujuh.

Al-Jannah (the Garden) is intended to mean the totality of the abode of true reward, comprising many gardens; or it is intended as a genus, like ﴿a soul will know﴾ [al-Takwir: 14].

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿like a garden on a hill﴾ [al-Baqarah: 265]. That increases the beauty of its interior with the beauty of the scenes that the one dwelling in it beholds, and this is a description encompassing the beauty of the Garden's location.

[Page 300]

*al-Lāghiyah* is a verbal noun meaning *al-laghw* (idle, vain talk), like *al-kādhibah* for *al-kadhib* (lie) and *al-khā'inah* and *al-'āfiyah*. The meaning is: no idle talk is heard in it. Alternatively, it is an adjective describing an implied feminine noun, meaning "a vain word," referring to what the word *lāghiyah* indicates, namely that they are words. Describing the word as *lāghiyah* is a metonymy of the intellect (*majāz 'aqlī*), since the one who is idle is its speaker.

The negation of hearing idle talk is a metonymy for the absence of idle talk in Paradise, of the type found in the line:

*"And you do not see the lizard (ḍabb) therein retreating into its hole."*

That is, there is no lizard there, since the lizard does not fail to retreat into its hole.

*Al-laghw* is speech that has no benefit. This is a reminder that Paradise is a realm of seriousness and truth, so no speech is uttered there except for a benefit, because souls there have been freed from all deficiencies. *"Alas for Zayyāba, for the warrior who attacks at dawn, then the one who takes the spoils, then the one who returns."*

Al-Suhaylī said: "Conjoining with *thumma* (then) is far-fetched." Al-Damāmīnī said: "Likewise in clauses: 'I passed by a man who memorizes the Qur'an, knows jurisprudence, and fears God.'" He said: "Al-Wāḥidī stated, regarding the Almighty's saying: *'O you who believe, do not take as intimates others than yourselves; they will not spare you [from] corruption; they love what distresses you. The attributes of Paradise begin with its essential attribute, which is that it is lofty (*'āliyah*). It is followed by the attribute of its being exalted above what counts as deficiencies of gatherings of people and dwellings of communities, namely clamour and idle talk. This clause has been left unconjoined to *'āliyah* out of regard for the lack of compatibility between single words and clauses, and this rightly calls for non-conjunction, because it is stronger than complete disconnection in the conjoining of clauses.

This is an attribute of Paradise, describing the goodness of its inhabitants.

[Page 301]

Nāfi' read *lā tusma'u* with a *tā'* (ت) that is dotted above and vowelled with a *ḍammah*, and *lāghiyatun* as the deputy subject (*nā'ib fā'il*). Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr, and Ruways from Ya'qūb read it with a *yā'* (ي) dotted below and vowelled with a *ḍammah*, and also with *lāghiyatun* in the nominative. The verb is thus treated as masculine, because *lāghiyah* is not of real feminine gender. This was made good by the separation that occurs between the verb and the noun it is attributed to. Ibn 'Āmir, 'Āṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Abū Ja'far, and Rawḥ from Ya'qūb read it with a *fatḥah* on the *tā'* (ت) and with the accusative *(lāghiyatan)*, and the *tā'* is for addressing an unspecified addressee.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 88, verse 12:

﴿Therein is a flowing spring.﴾

It is a third attribute of "jannah" (garden). The intended meaning is the category of springs, as in His saying, ﴿Every soul will know what it has presented﴾ [al-Takwir: 14], meaning: souls will know. This is a description of the Garden through its possessing the finest qualities of gardens, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or you will have a garden of palm trees and grapevines, and you will make rivers gush forth within them abundantly﴾ [al-Isra': 91].

It was not conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the sentence before it because the two differ in form: the first is a verbal sentence (fi'liyyah) and the second a nominal sentence (ismiyyah). This difference is among the embellishments of disconnection (husn al-fasl). Moreover, the sentence ﴿Therein they hear no idle talk﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 11] is intended to affirm the Garden's freedom from deficiencies (tanzzuh 'an al-naqa'if), while the sentence ﴿Therein is a flowing spring﴾ is intended to affirm some of its excellences.

**Verses 13–16:** ﴿Therein are raised couches,﴾ ﴿and cups set in place,﴾ ﴿and cushions arranged in rows,﴾ ﴿and carpets spread out.﴾

A fourth description of the Garden (jannah).

The phrase "therein" (fīhā) is repeated rather than joining "couches" to "a spring" (ʿayn) by simple conjunction, because joining the couches to the spring would sound awkward to the ear, since the mind would have to bring together the spring of water and the couches, unless the Garden itself gathers them. For this reason the adverbial phrase "therein" is repeated, to make clear that this containment is what unites them. Also, there is a difference between the containment of the flowing spring in the Garden and the containment of the couches and what is conjoined to them, namely the furnishings of the palaces and the household goods. That is why "cups," "cushions," and "carpets" are conjoined, since they are alike in being among the furnishings of the superb dwellings.

[Page 302]

This is a description of the Garden's excellences through the excellences of the furnishings of its palaces. The pronoun in "therein" refers to the Garden, on the basis that what is in its palaces is contained in it through an intermediary.

*Sururun* is the plural of *sarīr*, which is that on which one sits or reclines, and which is wide enough for a reclining person. It is made of wood or iron and has legs so that it is raised above the ground. Since elevation above the ground is part of the concept of the *sarīr*, describing them as "raised" (*marfūʿa*) serves to depict their beauty.

*Akwāb* is the plural of *kūb* (with the *k* vowelled with a *ḍamma*), a vessel for wine that has a stem (handle-less, with no loop). *Mawḍūʿa* means that they are not removed from before them as drinking vessels are removed in this world when the drinkers reach the limit of intoxication from consuming wine. The term "placed" (*mawḍūʿa*) is used as a metonymy (*kināya*) for the uninterrupted enjoyment of drink, in taste and in the pleasure it brings; that is, they are "placed" with the drinks that are in them.

There is an appearance of antithesis (*ṭibāq*) between "raised" (*marfūʿa*) and "placed" (*mawḍūʿa*), because the literal meaning of "raising" is the opposite of the literal meaning of "placing." There is no real opposition between the figurative use of the first and the literal use of the second, but it gives the appearance of opposition.

*Namāriq* is the plural of *numruqa* (with the *n* vowelled with a *ḍamma*, and a *sukūn* on the *m*, followed by a *rāʾ* with a *ḍamma*), which is the cushion upon which the seated or reclining person leans.

*Maṣfūfa* means that some of them are placed close to others in a row; that is, wherever the one seated wishes to sit, he finds one.

*Zarābiyy* is the plural of *zarbiyya* (with a *fatḥa* on the *z*, a *sukūn* on the *r*, a *kasra* on the *b*, and a *shadda* on the *y*), which is a rug or a *ṭunfusa* (with a *ḍamma* on the *ṭ*), woven from colourful, soft wool, spread on the ground for adornment and for sitting upon, for people of luxury and wealth.

The word *zarbiyya* is a nisba (relative adjective) to (Ādharbayjān), a land among the lands of Persia and Bukhara. The original form of *zarbiyya* was *adharbiyya*, whose *hamza* was dropped for lightness, because the name was heavy on account of its foreignness and the attachment of the nisba *yā'*. Its *dhāl* is substituted for a *zāy* in the speech of the Arabs; for the name of the land in the Persian tongue is *Āzarbayjān*, with a *zāy* followed by a *rāʾ*, and there is no *dhāl* in Persian speech. The land of (Ādharbayjān) is famous for the softness of its sheep's wool, and it is also renowned for the fine craftsmanship of its rugs and carpets and the delicacy of their pile.

[Page 303]

*Mabthūṯa* means spread out over the ground in abundance, and this implies a metonymy (*kināya*) for abundance.

The descriptions of the faces of the people of the Fire have been set against the descriptions of the faces of the people of the Garden. Thus the descriptions "humbled, labouring, weary" are set against "pleasant," and "[pleased] with their striving" [al-Ghashiyah: 9]. This is a promise to the believers that in the Garden they will have what they recognize of blessings in this world, and they know that the luxury of the Garden cannot be reached by description in speech. This is gathered in a general way in His saying, "Therein is what the souls desire and what the eyes delight in" [al-Zukhruf: 71]. But the spirits find rest in what is familiar to them, so they are given it, and it becomes for the spirits of people in every age and from every land the utmost degree of blessing in what they were accustomed to, especially what is familiar to all people of civilization and luxury and what they used to long for in this world. Then they will be increased in blessing beyond what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human being.

Surat al-Fajr

There has been no disagreement about naming this surah (Surat al-Fajr) without the waw, in the codices, the exegeses, and the books of Sunnah.

It is Meccan by consensus, except what Ibn 'Atiyya related from Abu 'Amr al-Dani, that he related from some scholars that it is Medinan.

It has been counted the tenth in the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Layl and before Surat al-Duha.

The number of its verses is thirty-two according to the counters of Medina and Mecca, who counted His saying ﴿and bestowed favours upon him﴾ (wa-na'ammahu) as the end of a verse, and His saying ﴿his provision﴾ (rizqahu) as the end of a verse. Others did not count them as the end of a verse. It is thirty according to the counters of Kufa and Syria, and twenty-nine according to the counters of Basra.

The people of Syria counted ﴿brought Hell﴾ (bi-jahannam) as the end of a verse, and the people of Kufa counted ﴿among My servants﴾ (fi 'ibadi) as the end of a verse.

* * *

It contains the following themes: setting forth a parable for the polytheists of Mecca in their turning away from accepting the message of their Lord, by the example of 'Ad, Thamud, and the people of Pharaoh;

warning them of the punishment of the Hereafter;

strengthening the Prophet (ﷺ) together with the promise of the destruction of his enemies;

and nullifying the delusion of the polytheists of Mecca, who suppose that the bounty they are in is a sign that Allah has honoured them, and that the poverty in which the believers live is a sign that Allah has humiliated them.

Surat al-Fajr

There has been no disagreement about naming this surah (Surat al-Fajr) without the waw, in the codices, the exegeses, and the books of Sunnah.

It is Meccan by consensus, except what Ibn 'Atiyya related from Abu 'Amr al-Dani, that he related from some scholars that it is Medinan.

It has been counted the tenth in the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Layl and before Surat al-Duha.

The number of its verses is thirty-two according to the counters of Medina and Mecca, who counted His saying ﴿and bestowed favours upon him﴾ (wa-na'ammahu) as the end of a verse, and His saying ﴿his provision﴾ (rizqahu) as the end of a verse. Others did not count them as the end of a verse. It is thirty according to the counters of Kufa and Syria, and twenty-nine according to the counters of Basra.

The people of Syria counted ﴿brought Hell﴾ (bi-jahannam) as the end of a verse, and the people of Kufa counted ﴿among My servants﴾ (fi 'ibadi) as the end of a verse.

* * *

It contains the following themes: setting forth a parable for the polytheists of Mecca in their turning away from accepting the message of their Lord, by the example of 'Ad, Thamud, and the people of Pharaoh;

warning them of the punishment of the Hereafter;

strengthening the Prophet (ﷺ) together with the promise of the destruction of his enemies;

and nullifying the delusion of the polytheists of Mecca, who suppose that the bounty they are in is a sign that Allah has honoured them, and that the poverty in which the believers live is a sign that Allah has humiliated them.

And that they have squandered the thanks due to Allah for the blessing, so they did not share some of it with the weak, and it only increased them in greed for accumulating more of it.

And that on the Day of Resurrection they will regret not having sent forward for themselves deeds that would benefit them, on a day when no soul will benefit from its wealth, and nothing will benefit it except its faith and its affirmation of the promise of its Lord; and that benefits the believers in their destination, which is Paradise.
